name: Jaqaru
catalog_quote: Stress in Jaqaru is non-phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate vowel of the word and is frequently accompanied by a rise in pitch. In words of three vowels or more, a secondary stress occurs before the main stress. Hardman (1966:26).Vowel length is phonemic: c'aka 'bone' vs. c'a:ka 'chest'.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Jaqaru is usually penultimate, but it is antepenultimate in loans that were consonant-final and stressed on the penult in the donor language. A final vowel is added to avoid a consonant-final root. The added vowel usually copies the preceding one, as in (2), yielding 'epenthesis' copy harmony. [...] (2) [i] mártisi < martes (Spanish) 'Tuesday' [...] [a] húpasa < uvas (Spanish) 'grapes' [...] [u] áxusu < ajos (Spanish) 'garlic' / ríluxu < reloj (Spanish) 'watch'. When these loans are suffixed, stress shifts to the penult.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 penultimate stress = penultimate). Adds the loan-stratum exception (antepenult in vowel-augmented consonant-final loans, reverting to penult under suffixation) and the fact that stress interacts with vowel copy harmony (the stressed vowel copies a following suffix vowel).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. The one systematic exception is consonant-final loans from Spanish and Quechua: they receive a paragogic (copy) final vowel and keep the donor-language stress, which then surfaces on the antepenult (mártisi, áxusu, ríluxu); once such a loan takes a suffix, stress moves back to the penult (axusí-ni ~ axsú-ni). The paper is a 4-page OT abstract about copy harmony; the stress statement is a one-sentence background generalization with examples, not a dedicated stress section.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress in consonant-final loans that were penult-stressed in the donor language and received an added final vowel (Spanish martes > mártisi, uvas > húpasa, ajos > áxusu, reloj > ríluxu; Quechua qanchis > qánchisi, qallay > qállaya); stress returns to the penult when these loans are suffixed. Data attributed to Cerrón-Palomino (2000 and p.c.).
new_statements.identity_note: Walker 2010 treats Jaqaru as a single language (Aymaran, Peru; Tupe) with data from Cerrón-Palomino 2000 and p.c; no dialect is named. Not about Kawki/Cauqui.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding texts are confirmed in copies we hold — Hardman 1969's sentence verbatim on PDF p. 3 of the ERIC scan we hold, and the StressTyp2 passage verbatim in the held the StressTyp2 entry for this language. But the classification ultimately rests on a database paraphrase of Hardman 1966:26 plus a one-sentence conference handout; none of Hardman's three grammars is held, so 'best available held' = no. Penultimate default is secure across every source seen (Hardman 1966 via StressTyp2, Hardman 1969, Cerrón-Palomino 1994, Walker 2010). The 'strict' flag is the exposed part: the record's own Walker quotation already reports antepenultimate stress in consonant-final loans, StressTyp2's Hardman paraphrase says 'normally', and Cerrón-Palomino 1994 (downloaded now, pp. 76-77) states the accent is 'básicamente' penultimate but sensitive to underlying form and word-internal structure, with antepenultimate loans
